Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: The absence of a specific skin rash commonly associated with SLE might seem contradictory, but SLE can present with a wide range of symptoms
Negative HIV and tuberculin skin testing, while important to rule out other diseases, do not contradict SLE diagnosis
CT scans and axillary lymph node biopsy being negative for malignancy do not directly contradict SLE, as SLE is an autoimmune disease, not a malignancy
Demographics and symptoms can align with SLE, which is more common in women
Progressive generalized weakness, weight loss, and dyspnea could be indicative of a systemic disease like SLE
Mucosal pallor and non-tender lymphadenopathy can be seen in SLE
Initial laboratory findings such as anemia (Hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL) and leukopenia (White blood cell count 3.5 ×10^9/L) are consistent with SLE
Presence of high titers of ANA, anti–double-stranded DNA, and anti–Smith antibodies with low complement C3 levels strongly supports SLE diagnosis
Acute inflammatory arthritis, urinalysis showing pH 5, 16 WBCs and 27 RBCs per high-power field, and 24-hour urinary protein 0.81 g/day are consistent with SLE
Recurring leukopenia and estimated glomerular filtration rate of 53 mL/min/1.73 m^2 also support SLE
